reviews.text:
I had my tortoise examined.

They listened carefully to all my questions, and the treatment was completed quickly, which was great.

The clinic was also very clean.

I was looking for a veterinary clinic that treats snakes and found this one.

Actually, even though they're called "animal" clinics, most only treat dogs (it's a dog's paradise these days), so there are very few clinics that treat other animals.

And the number of clinics that treat exotic animals or reptiles is even smaller, and the number of clinics that treat snakes is even smaller.

It just goes to show how unpopular snakes are...

Yet, this clinic was able to accurately treat the sores, abscesses, and parasites of a strange snake from the dark continent of Africa.

Thank you so much!

Of course, their main patients are dogs and cats, but when I saw the turtle in the tank on the reception counter...

Well, anyone who can immediately identify that species is probably a serious enthusiast. Including myself.

Postscript: I used their services again in October 2026 for a different snake.

I was surprised to find that they had moved from their previous location to a stylish building, and that the number of staff had increased dramatically.
However, I was very grateful that they were able to perform surgery on the same day.
I was worried because the snake was elderly, but I'm extremely thankful that everything turned out alright.
Thank you very much.

I appreciate your reply, but since this happened over two years ago, there might be errors in the medical records or they may have mistaken me for the wrong patient. I'm very disappointed.

If they had explained this at the time, there wouldn't have been a problem. The problem with this hospital isn't the equipment, but the lack of explanation to patients.

I was referred to an animal hospital in Adachi Ward. It's an hour and a half each way. The hospital recommended a hospital with more advanced technology, citing reasons such as greater safety and lower risk if CT scans and surgery are done at the same hospital.

I felt like I was being refused treatment because I was recommended another hospital during the consultation process.

A long time ago, the director and vice-director always explained things very carefully, and sometimes even wrote notes on important points.

______________________________________________
Previously, I received treatment from the director and vice-director, and it was a very thorough and trustworthy hospital.

This time, the doctor was typing on the computer the entire time during the consultation. When I asked a question, they would look up and answer a word or two, but then go back to typing. It seemed like they were busy with data entry and treating the patient half-heartedly.

This hospital doesn't perform CT scans on dogs, so they recommended another hospital an hour away.

It's a hospital with a good reputation, so it seems I just happened to get a bad doctor.

The building is clean and well-maintained, but I got the impression that they focused too much on the exterior and neglected the quality of the doctors.

When I went for a check-up for my hedgehog, they said they couldn't do anything because it curled up. What should I do if my hedgehog curls up?

I had my reptile examined here.

They listened to my concerns very attentively. They thoroughly explained the risks of the procedure, which put my mind at ease. After the procedure, they also explained various possibilities and carefully instructed me on how to treat it at home.

While I had to wait for an appointment everywhere else, this clinic has many veterinarians, many of whom can treat unusual animals, so I was able to get an appointment right away.

I visited the vet again this time for a check-up for my cat. It was a different doctor than last time (this time it was a female doctor), but she examined my cat very attentively. She considered both my needs and my cat's needs when discussing treatment options. I was also grateful that she spoke to my cat very gently during the treatment. I'm so glad to have a reliable animal hospital in my neighborhood.

This is a truly wonderful hospital where they treat animals with genuine care.
I appreciate that they also treat hedgehogs and other unusual animals (exotic animals).
The separate entrances and waiting rooms for cats and dogs are also excellent.

They are all very kind, thorough, and excellent doctors.

They are all overflowing with love for animals, and my rabbit is always calm and not scared at the vet, so I feel at ease during examinations.

Previously, Dr. Naruse bandaged my rabbit's sore hocks, and he did a very careful job—not too loose, not too tight—and made sure the affected area wasn't touching the floor. He was a very kind and trustworthy doctor.

I'm writing this because what happened during my second visit was shocking.

The photo shows my bird's claws two days after it recovered.

It's a one-year-old White-bellied Caique.

My first visit was at the end of summer, when the intense heat had subsided. I went for a claw trim, beak care, and its first health checkup.

I chose this hospital for my first visit because of the many positive reviews.

The doctor was a young man who responded to the bird's calls with a "yes," spoke gently, and gave me his business card, leaving a very positive and trustworthy impression. I went for a health checkup, but I was told that if there were no concerns, they didn't need to do anything stressful like X-rays, so I only requested a stool sample test. I was called back after what felt like 15-20 minutes.

My bird seemed tired from its first hospital visit! When I got home, it ate normally and there were no problems, so I decided I would use their services again.


Second visit, early November
Appointment for feather trimming, nail trimming, and beak trimming
Since the bird itself didn't seem to mind, I trusted the previous vet and made a specific appointment.
A different female vet came out.
I wondered why, but I assumed that the vet I had specifically requested would trim the nails, so I explained my needs and left the bird with her.
At this time, the vet didn't introduce herself.
Furthermore, she asked if there were any abnormalities with the droppings or urine, but I said "pee and poop."
Don't people usually say poop or feces?
After I left the bird,
I heard a tremendous bird cry. Of course, it cried last time too, but it was much cuter. This time, the cries were clearly from someone who hated it. I listened, thinking, "It must hate having its wings trimmed..." After what felt like 20 minutes, I was called back into the examination room.
There was a chilling amount of blood on the white feathers on its belly and the yellow feathers on its legs, and the nails were all different lengths, and one nail was missing? My beloved bird was there, thrashing about terribly because its claws were so short.

The vet apologized for causing bleeding during the nail trimming, but said it was fine because he'd administered a hemostatic agent.

And that was it.

When I returned my bird to its cage from the vet's cage, it was terrified of the vet, crying and thrashing about.

At the checkout, I mentioned that I'd requested a specific vet but it was a different one.

They said it was an emergency and the vet wasn't available, so it was a substitute! They cheerfully said they'd let the vet I'd booked know about the visit.

I went home with some doubts, thinking, "Well, I guess that happens sometimes?"

It was perched on a tree, tilted more than usual, with its painful leg raised.

It was repeatedly shaking its head from side to side, a strange movement I'd never seen before.

Looking at it again, the condition of its claws was terrible, and it looked so painful that I cried.

I went to the vet because I was worried about trimming its claws myself, so I'm furious that it ended up like this.


Looking back, it was incredibly suspicious that the doctor didn't introduce himself at the beginning, saying something like, "The doctor scheduled for today couldn't make it, so I'll be taking over. I'm [Name]." I should have asked properly from the start.

The way he said "poop," and instead of apologizing, he said "I'm sorry,"

His choice of words, the sincerity of his apology, and even his personality, made me unable to accept him, even before considering him as a doctor.

I should have asked him on the spot about the situation and circumstances that led to the claws being so short they were bleeding and almost gone.

The fact that his apology was just a report, not a genuine apology, makes me furious and wonder if he's really fit to be a doctor.

Many pet owners trim their birds' claws themselves, but I'm scared, so I always ask the vet to do it. This defeats the purpose of asking them to do it, doesn't it?

I took a taxi door-to-door to avoid stressing the bird. Including medical expenses, this total cost will exceed 10,000 yen.

I'm filled with regret today, having spent money only to stress my beloved bird.

Regarding my first encounter with my bird:
My bird didn't reject the male veterinarian during the first consultation and didn't struggle. (Of course, it was nervous.)
With the second veterinarian, it struggled and cried from the first meeting and was out of breath.
I now understand why the bird struggled before anything even began; perhaps it disliked this veterinarian from the start.
Even though there was bleeding and I was worried, the veterinarian spoke cheerfully and clearly throughout. I wondered if he had any human feelings.

I had a good impression of the male veterinarian, and his claws were trimmed evenly without being over-cut. The cage transfer was smooth, and the bird didn't struggle violently at the end.

I plan to request the same male veterinarian for the third nail trim.
If it were any other veterinarian, I would leave without hesitation.

As this is my first pet, my knowledge is limited and I have much to reflect on, but because we are caring for animals that cannot speak human language, it's essential to find a veterinarian I can trust and like 200%. I understand that compatibility is important, so I won't say the vet is entirely bad, but this particular vet is a no-go. I've decided that if even 1% of something bothers me, I'll ask until I'm satisfied, and if I'm still not convinced, I won't entrust my pet to them.

When you carefully read the negative reviews, you'll find comments about vets who shirk responsibility or fail to tell you the facts.

I felt the same way this time.

The staff profiles on their website all mention animals, and their photos show them with animals.
This initially gave me a good impression.

However, this experience has made me wonder if some vets don't actually like animals that much, or lack empathy, and if their "love for animals and caring for them with genuine care" image is just an appeal. It's actually made me distrustful...
Because if they truly cared, they would at least provide a proper explanation, right?

Of course, vets are human too, so they'll have animals they don't like, and I don't expect all of them to love animals.

But I had no choice but to entrust my pet to the vet.

This time, it wasn't for treatment, but just for trimming the claws, beak, and feathers.

I didn't need to overthink it; I just wanted them to do it calmly, and everything should be fine.

Clean conduct, doing your best.
Please try your best to abide by these.
Thank you.

I will also be checking out the new hospital.

▼Added on June 30, 2026
When I mentioned this at another hospital, they said that sometimes they cut the nails so short that they bleed because it's dangerous if they get caught on something. They didn't explain that at the time, so I didn't know...

At another hospital, they cut my nails so short that they bled a little, but not this short, so I can't deny that I cut them too short.

I received treatment for my hamster. The examination results showed that a complete recovery was unlikely, but the doctor in charge explained the possible diagnoses, examination methods, and treatment options in an easy-to-understand manner.
I'm grateful for the courteous response I received in the emergency room.
Patient and very nice vets 🐶 …

Even exotic animals like goats come to this clinic.

They treat all kinds of animals, not just dogs and cats.

They're generally open every day of the week, so if something happens to your family member,

go right away.

There are reviews saying it's expensive, but it's cheaper if you have insurance.

Well, my rabbit is elderly so I don't have insurance for him, but
it costs 20,000 yen a month for molar maintenance, anesthesia, X-rays, a consultation with the vet, and medication.

Rabbits are relatively expensive, so that's normal.

My bearded dragon, whom I've had for eight years, suddenly had a seizure the other day (the first time he'd ever been sick since I got him). I frantically contacted a nearby animal hospital, and they referred me to this one. Despite it being a Sunday, they were incredibly helpful over the phone and were able to see him right away.

They listened attentively to my concerns and, after seizure medication, oxygen, X-rays, and blood tests, prescribed medication for the suspected illness.

After giving him the medication, he gradually recovered, day after day, and made a remarkable recovery!

Seeing my bearded dragon suffering so much, I had almost given up hope, but thanks to this doctor, he recovered, and I'm truly grateful.

I'm so glad I took him to this hospital.
They're just focusing on the exterior. Don't expect any decent service. There are other veterinary clinics nearby, so I recommend them.

The director, Dr. Matsubara, is a truly trustworthy and excellent doctor.
He's not in my neighborhood, but I've been taking care of him since my previous dog was born. There have been some negative reviews, and as an animal hospital with multiple veterinarians on staff, some people may have a negative impression, but Dr. Matsubara's diagnostic imaging and surgery are top-notch.
He's also happy to provide second opinions, and will answer even minor questions over the phone. As my family doctor for many years, I have the utmost trust in him and leave it to him.
I've seen reviews saying the prices are high, but I can't help but wonder if those people would rather go to a hospital that uses old equipment and hasn't made much investment in facilities. The prices are proportional to the constant updating of equipment. I don't think it's just animal hospitals, though.

I've been to your clinic many times for my reptiles.
The other day, I thought something was wrong so I went in.
They ran various tests and treated my reptile, but its symptoms worsened. It even started to show nerve damage, so I had to take it in for a quick visit.
The reptile already looked exhausted, and to be honest, I had almost given up, but the doctor said, "We don't want to give up yet," and I almost cried.
After the treatment, it became noticeably healthier and the nerve damage disappeared.

There are very few hospitals that are able to accommodate sudden requests and perform various tests and treatments, so it's a great help.

This hospital has operational problems. First of all, the entrance is hard to find, the procedure of changing into slippers before entering is also confusing, and furthermore, perhaps to save on labor costs, there is no one inside, and no one comes out even when called. The building is confusing and difficult to use, and the flow of people is a mess. There is no one in charge of managing the hospital, so unless you contact them yourself, you will not receive any communication regarding test results. With this system in place, I am worried about the nighttime care for hospitalized pets and the communication system in case of a critical condition.

I had my bearded dragon examined.

Before coming here, I went to three other vets, but each time I went, they said the symptoms were different, and despite treatment, it didn't get any better. They were giving me vague diagnoses like "it's okay for a month even if it's not eating" or "this isn't a problem," and it actually got worse, so I came here.

The examination was very thorough, and they explained the treatment plan and costs, which was reassuring.

It was in a pretty bad state, but I'm relieved that the runaround is finally over.

I regret not coming here sooner...
Thank you so much for the thorough examination.

I had my budgie examined here.

They were able to identify the cause of the ailment that other clinics couldn't pinpoint, and provided appropriate treatment.

It's reassuring to know that they can perform bird X-rays so smoothly, as there aren't many animal hospitals that can do that.

The clinic is clean and reassuring, and if you make an appointment, the waiting time isn't too long, which is a great help.

I've received a lot of care here. I've had owls, bats, crows, frogs, leopard geckos, snakes, and Japanese rhinoceros beetle lizards treated here, and I've especially owed them a lot of care. When you have a lot of exotic animals like me, there are only a limited number of hospitals to choose from, so this is a big help.

Thank you for taking care of my golden hamster.

Initially, I brought him in for a check-up, but the care was incredibly thorough, and they detected a hormonal disorder early on.

Although he passed away, I believe that the staff at Vanquet noticed a change in his breathing during his last visit, allowing for palliative care and a peaceful end.

I believe that my hamster, who was small from the start and had a chronic illness, was able to live to 2 years and 8 months old thanks to all the staff at Vanquet. Thank you so much for everything.

I called to make a reservation because the reviews were good.

The man's attitude was arrogant and condescending,
which was very unpleasant and somewhat shocking.

I received excellent care for my reptile 🦎.

The doctor was incredibly kind, and I was surprised when he spoke to my reptile 🦎 when it became agitated during the examination. Sadly, it was too late, and the 🦎 passed away.

When I called to inform him of this, the doctor himself kindly took the phone and explained the situation to me. 🥲
At previous hospitals, the receptionist would only say, "I'll let the director know," so I was both surprised and filled with gratitude.

I've decided to entrust my other reptiles to this doctor as well.
My Greater Siren pup had something on his skin, so I took him to the vet. After he was examined, it healed in just one week! I'm so grateful to the doctor.
There are teachers and staff who are very skilled at cutting rabbit nails. They are very experienced and great at handling rabbits. They even do it well on my rambunctious rabbits.

I am receiving care at Guinea Pig. 
All the doctors are very kind and considerate in their examinations.

After going to many different hospitals, I finally found Vanket. Vanket is so well-known around here that when you think of animal hospitals, you think of Vanket. My French Bulldog has had surgery and been hospitalized due to illness and accidentally ingesting something, but he recovers quickly, so I can trust him with their care. The doctors and nurses are very kind and I've never had a bad experience. 
They responded quickly in an emergency.
I'm so glad that there is a doctor who treats African dormice! The treatment and medication prescriptions are always accurate and helpful. I look forward to working with you again in the future!

My cats are being cared for here. The facilities are clean and the doctors are kind and explain things to me in a gentle manner. They are attentive to both the cats and the owners, so I can leave them in their care with peace of mind. They have also achieved gold level as a cat-friendly clinic.
The clinic director is also well-versed in exotic animals, so I think it would be a good place for exotic owners who are unsure where to take their pets.

I'm sorry to say this, but while I haven't been involved with all the staff at this hospital, I've been taking my pet there for visits for 10 months, about once a month, and for the first time in January, it was hospitalized for 4 days. However, I saw absolutely no compassion for the animals.

Based on the reviews, I wondered if they really specialize in exotic animals...?

I was completely dissatisfied with the treatment and handling, and I was planning to transfer my pet to another hospital first thing in the morning... but it ended in the worst possible way.

I noticed this from the beginning of my visits, but four times, despite making reservations by phone and in person, my reservations weren't recorded. On top of that, they mixed up the dog's food with the cat's food.

You absolutely must make reservations online here.

Their website says they have all the necessary equipment, but for some reason, there were no cameras in the ICU, and it seems no one stays to monitor the animals even when they're in poor condition.

(Apparently, they installed six cameras two days after my child's accident.)
Why didn't they install cameras when they could have? The director said it was because they hadn't had an accident like my child's in the 12 years since opening, but I think crisis management is about taking preventative measures, and it seems that wasn't done.
Furthermore, at this hospital, there was a male staff member whose forehead was clearly visible and inappropriate for public display...
I was shocked, thinking, "At a hospital?!"
At the very least, they should have covered it properly.

My Pomeranian, who just turned 17, has chronic pancreatitis. He developed acute renal failure and high CRP levels from the pancreatitis, and was hospitalized for 6 days at an emergency hospital. His acute renal failure levels returned to their previous levels, and his CRP, which was quite high, dropped to 2. His lipase levels were still a little high, so we transferred him to this hospital, which has been our regular vet for the past 10 months.
He's currently in the ICU.

I only realized this after my pet was hospitalized, but even though we visited every day, not a single staff member offered a word of explanation about my pet's condition during its stay.

Day by day, it felt like they were just watching without offering any real information.

The hospital director was in charge, and although we contacted them before visiting, despite the poor test results, they didn't say anything to us, the pet owners.

From the third day of hospitalization, the previously stable test results began to worsen.

When we visited, my pet, who usually reacts excitedly and kicks its legs when we see it, was lethargic and unresponsive.

A young male doctor, filling in for the director who was on leave, showed us the blood test results but offered almost no explanation. We pointed out the elevated inflammation levels, but it was brushed off.

From that moment on, I was filled with distrust.
The next day, I was incredibly anxious. After finishing work, I went to visit my child.
A male staff member guided me, saying, "This way," and to my shock, I saw my child clenching their teeth, their tongue sticking out,
suffering more than I had ever seen them before. Even more shocking was that the male staff member who guided me didn't even notice my child right in front of them.
I started to feel a little angry.
I immediately called another staff member, who then brought the doctor.
But the hospital director simply said, "I'll check the lungs and heart later." That was all. He said, "The breathing is fine."

No, no, it's not that they're having trouble breathing; they're probably in pain from pancreatitis. There was no pain medication, treatment, or tests in front of me.
On top of that, I glanced at the test results he was holding, and the inflammation level had risen to 12.9, more than four times what it was when we transferred. They also had a fever.
Don't they normally take the time to discuss the future treatment plan?

Since there was nothing else available, I spoke to them, and they said they hadn't changed the dosage of the medication prescribed by the emergency room, and since his condition was worsening, I asked if they could change the medication or temporarily increase the dosage, but all I got was a "hmm."

I wasn't satisfied.
I decided to transfer him to the emergency room tomorrow morning.
I was worried, so I called that night and left a voicemail. Apparently the hospital director was there, but didn't notice me and left without checking the voicemail.
He said he would check his lungs and heart later, but despite the sudden deterioration, he didn't contact me. I think that's incredibly dishonest.
And then... when I arrived this morning, he had passed away...
It's the worst possible outcome.
They only gave him painkillers and an injection to prevent blood clots and then sent him home.
What was the point of hospitalization? Injections can be done on an outpatient basis, right? Especially after such a sudden deterioration in his condition the day before. It seems they gave the injection without checking on the child's condition and left less than 30 minutes later. My child must have suffered alone for over 10 hours, unnoticed by anyone. I feel incredibly sorry for my child.

While they offered a full apology, I feel that most of the staff here have a low level of awareness.

When I went to speak with them, I immediately heard loud laughter from the staff behind the door. They knew what I was there to discuss, yet they were still laughing.

And the director couldn't even correct them.

They said they'll be holding monthly meetings from now on, but I was shocked that they weren't even doing that before.
